provocation

/prov-uh-KAY-shun/ - the stress falls on KAY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Provocation means an act intended to trigger an angry reaction.

Diplomats are trained to read an insult twice before treating it as provocation rather than clumsiness.

Worked Example

The playground monitor's report is a small masterpiece of observation. The older boy, it notes, never touched anyone. He held the cap just out of reach, wondered aloud whose sister had sewn the patch on it, and stood so that the teacher's sightline began exactly where the smaller boy's swing would land. The swing came. Only one child was marched inside.

Provocation is the exact word for the cap game, because a provocation is an act intended to trigger an angry reaction — the reaction is the product. An insult wants to wound and is finished; a provocation wants an answer, preferably a punishable one, and stages itself where the answer will cost the most.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

goading: Goading is needling that wants a reaction and keeps at it — jab after jab until the temper finally gives. A provocation can be a single staged act, finished in one stroke; goading is the drawn-out version that refuses to stop until you snap.

baiting: Baiting dangles something tempting — the unguarded pawn, the insult left hanging — and waits for the snap. A provocation needs no lure at all: it is an act built to trigger the angry reaction directly, pushed in front of you rather than left for you to take.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

olive branch: the offered peace itself

courtesy: the manners that give tempers nothing to feed on

Where it sits · how close to open aggression it comes — slight → provocation → attack

slight vs. provocation: A slight is far milder than a provocation: small enough to swallow — a skipped hello, a forgotten name, and possibly no harm meant at all — while a provocation takes aim at your temper on purpose.

attack vs. provocation: Attack goes further than provocation — a provocation is staged so that you strike first; an attack skips the theater and strikes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro-

Prefix — pro-: forth, out

Root — voc

Root — voc: voice, to call (Latin vocare)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the act of

Put it together

Put it together: Pro- (forth) + voc (to call) + -ation (the act of) = the act of calling forth. Latin provocare meant to call someone out — the challenge shouted across the arena — and the modern word keeps the dare in it: a provocation calls your anger out into the open, where it can be counted against you.

Use the root in a new word: vocal

Use the root in a new word: vocal: A vocal critic is simply one who gives the complaint voice — voc- doing its plainest work.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / judicial

Provocation is courtroom and chancellery vocabulary: it names the act that pulled the trigger of someone else's temper, and it often carries a plea inside it — he was provoked. A person who deals in it is provocative by design; the crowd-scale verb is this unit's incite. A mere insult wants to wound; a provocation wants your answer.
